questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A prolonged PT primarily measures platelet adhesion and aggregation, so the result most directly indicates a platelet-function disorder rather than a coagulation-factor abnormality.","B":"A prolonged PT primarily reflects the intrinsic pathway, making factor VIII and IX abnormalities the most direct explanation for the result when anticoagulants are not being used.","C":"A prolonged PT directly measures red-cell production, so the result most directly indicates impaired erythropoiesis rather than a defect involving coagulation factors.","D":"A prolonged PT reflects abnormalities in the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways and can occur with vitamin K deficiency, liver dysfunction, or coagulation-factor deficiency."}}
questions.rationale: PT evaluates the tissue-factor/extrinsic and common coagulation pathways and is standardized as INR for many clinical uses. Prolongation can occur with vitamin K deficiency, liver synthetic dysfunction, factor deficiencies, and anticoagulant effects. PT does not directly measure platelet function, red-cell production, or the intrinsic pathway measured by aPTT.
questions.source_name: MedlinePlus / NLM — Prothrombin Time and INR
questions.source_detail: PT measures time to clot formation through a different portion of the coagulation system than PTT and is used in evaluation of bleeding/coagulation disorders and warfarin effect.

questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A markedly elevated CRP identifies the exact infectious organism causing the client's illness, so culture or other diagnostic testing is unnecessary once the CRP result is known.","B":"A markedly elevated CRP specifically diagnoses an autoimmune disorder because infection, tissue injury, malignancy, and other inflammatory conditions do not meaningfully increase this marker.","C":"CRP is a nonspecific marker of inflammation that can rise with infection, injury, autoimmune disease, or other inflammatory states and must be interpreted with the overall clinical picture.","D":"CRP is primarily a marker of kidney filtration, so an elevated value should be interpreted as evidence of reduced glomerular filtration rather than evidence of systemic inflammation."}}
questions.rationale: CRP is produced by the liver in response to inflammation. An elevated CRP is nonspecific: it can accompany infection, tissue injury, autoimmune disease, and many other inflammatory conditions. The result must be interpreted with the history, examination, and other tests; it does not identify a specific diagnosis or organism.
questions.source_detail: MedlinePlus describes CRP as a blood marker that rises in response to inflammation from infection, injury, autoimmune disease and other causes.

questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An A1C of 9.5% is within the usual target for most nonpregnant adults, so treatment changes are generally unnecessary unless the client also reports recurrent hypoglycemia or symptoms.","B":"An A1C of 9.5% indicates glycemia well above the usual goal for many nonpregnant adults, but the treatment target should still be individualized to health status, preferences, and hypoglycemia risk.","C":"An A1C of 9.5% mainly indicates recurrent hypoglycemia because higher A1C values reflect excessive time below range rather than prolonged exposure to elevated glucose levels over several recent months.","D":"An A1C of 9.5% cannot provide useful information about recent glycemic exposure because A1C is used only to diagnose diabetes and not to monitor ongoing treatment effectiveness over time."}}
questions.rationale: The ADA 2026 Standards state that an A1C goal below 7% is appropriate for many nonpregnant adults, while goals should be individualized according to comorbidity, functional status, treatment burden, and hypoglycemia risk. An A1C of 9.5% is therefore substantially above the usual target for many adults, but treatment decisions remain individualized.
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association — Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026: Glycemic Goals
questions.source_detail: ADA 2026 recommends A1C <7% for many nonpregnant adults while emphasizing individualized goals and deintensification when treatment harms exceed benefits.

questions.rationale: CDC classifies adult BMI 30.0 to less than 35.0 kg/m² as Class 1 obesity. CDC also emphasizes that BMI is a screening measure rather than a stand-alone diagnosis of health or disease and should be considered with medical history, physical findings, behaviors, and other risk factors.
questions.source_detail: CDC: adult BMI 30.0–34.9 is Class 1 obesity; BMI is a screening measure and should be interpreted with other health information.

questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A high Morse score means every patient should receive the same fall-prevention bundle because the total score alone determines which interventions are effective for that individual.","B":"A high Morse score eliminates the need for repeat assessment because once high risk is documented, changes in medications, cognition, gait, or environment no longer alter the plan.","C":"A low Morse score guarantees that the patient will not fall, so staff can omit individualized prevention measures even when new dizziness or unsteady gait develops later.","D":"A higher Morse score indicates greater fall risk, but prevention should still target the patient's specific risk factors and be updated when the clinical situation changes."}}
questions.rationale: A higher Morse score indicates greater fall risk, but AHRQ's fall-prevention work warns against using the score alone to give every high-risk patient the same interventions. Effective prevention identifies patient-specific risk factors and implements a tailored plan that is reassessed when medications, gait, cognition, or clinical status change.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — Fall TIPS / Preventing Falls in Hospitals
questions.source_detail: AHRQ supports formal fall-risk assessment plus patient-specific interventions and notes that a score alone should not replace individualized clinical judgment.
